In accordance with WAC 456- 09- 955, Appellant has timely
filed a Petition for Review of the Initial Decision issued on May
2, 2002, following a hearing conducted on August 1, 2001, by the
Board of Tax Appeals ( Board).
In order for this' Board to reconsider the findings set forth
in the Initial Decision, it must be clear that the Initial
Decision did not properly consider the evidence or that there was
an omission of certain pertinent facts.
The Board reviewed the petition, the Initial Decision issued
concerning the appeal, and all available information and data.
We determine that the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
address the issues raised by Appellant in the petition.
This Board finds no basis for changing the Initial Decision.
We deny the Petition for Review.

8 III. -- APPLICABLE LAWS:
9
10 Within RCW 84. 36. 381 through 84. 36. 389, the Legislature estab-
11 lished the criteria whereby senior citizens qualify for property tax
12 exemptions. The Department of Revenue adopted rules and regulations,
13 WAC 458- 16- 010 through 458- 16- 079, to implement and administer the
14 above statutes. A person claiming an exemption must meet the occu-
15 pancy, ownership, age, and income provisions set forth within these
16 regulations. The parties agree Mr. Brabant meets the ownership, age,
17 and income elements for exemption qualification. The only disputed
18 issue is whether Mr. Brabant meets the occupancy requirements relative
19 to his Federal Way property for the 2000 tax year.
20
21 In relevant part, RCW 84. 36. 381 provides:
22 A person shall be exempt from any legal obligation to
pay all or a portion of the amount of excess and regular
23 real property taxes due and payable in the year following
the year in which a claim is filed, and thereafter, in
24 accordance with the following:
1) The property taxes must have been imposed upon a
25 residence which was occupied by the person claiming the
exemption as a principal place of residence as of the time
26 of filing: PROVIDED, That any person who sells, transfers,
or is displaced from his or her residence may transfer his
27 or her exemption status to a replacement residence, but
no claimant shall receive an exemption on more than one
INITIAL DECISION - Page 5 Docket No. 00- 068

1 residence in any year: PROVIDED FURTHER, That confinement
of the person to a hospital or nursing home shall not
2 disqualify the claim of exemption . . . .
3
4 RCW 84. 36. 383 defines residence, in part as:
5 1) The term " residence" shall mean a single family
dwelling unit whether such unit be separate or part of a
6 multiunit dwelling, including the land on which such
dwelling stands not to exceed one acre.
7
8
9 WAC 458- 16- 010 states, in part:
10 1) . . . The residence must have been occupied by
the person claiming the exemption as the principal or main
11 residence of the claimant. It does not include a residence
used merely as a vacation home. For purposes of this exemp-
12 tion, principal or main residence means a residence the
claimant resides at or dwells in for more than six months
13 each year. Items to be considered in verifying residency
can be ownership of another residence, voter registration
14 and vehicle licensing.
15
16 WAC 458- 16- 020 provides:
17 1) The property taxes must have been imposed upon
a residence which was occupied by the person claiming the
18 exemption as a principal place of residence as of January 1
of the year in which the claim is filed.
19
20
21 An exemption from taxation is to be construed narrowly. " Taxation
22 is the rule and exemption is the exception." O' Leary v. Department of
23 Revenue, 105 Wn. 2d 679, 717 P. 2d 273 ( 1986). Exemptions and deductions
24 are to be construed strictly in favor of the tax and, as a corollary,
25 they are not to be extended beyond the scope clearly indicated by the
26 legislature." Mac Amusement Co. v. Department of Revenue, 95 Wn. 2d
27 963, 633 P. 2d 68 ( 1981). Moreover, the taxpayer bears the burden of
INITIAL DECISION - Page 6 Docket No. 00- 068

1 establishing that it qualifies for the claimed exemption or deduction.
2 Group Health Coop. of Puget Sound, Inc. v. Department of Revenue, 106
3 Wn. 2d 391, 401- 02, 722 P. 2d 787 ( 1986).
4
5 Because he filed his exemption claim for his Federal Way property
6 in 1999, Mr. Brabant bears the burden of demonstrating clearly that as
7 of January 1, 1999, this was his principal place of residence and that
8 he resided there more than six months during 1999.

7 VIII. -- ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS:
8
9 As agreed by the parties and framed by the applicable laws, the
10 issue in this appeal is relatively narrow. Does the evidence provided
11 demonstrate clearly that as of January 1, 1999, Mr. Brabant' s Federal
12 Way property was his principal place of residence and did he reside
13 there more than six months that year?
14
15 The evidence advanced by Mr. Brabant confirms his Federal Way
16 residence was not a rental property during 1999 and that he spent some
17 time there during the year. However, given the evidence provided, the
18 Board is unable to quantify just how much time he was in residence at
19 his Federal Way property.
20
21 To support his Federal Way residency claim, Mr. Brabant relies on
22 a number of unsworn written statements, his Woodstone Credit Union
23 account, and a King County library card. There are problems with this
24 evidence. The written statements, in general, indicate Mr. Brabant
25 interacted with some Federal Way individuals, institutions, and busi-
26 nesses over the years. However, this information is not probative of
27 residency at this property during 1999. For example, the statement from
INITIAL DECISION - Page 14 Docket No. 00- 068

1 the appliance store owner indicates Mr. Brabant used this company for
2 his appliance servicing needs over the years. Yet, no dates of these
3 servicing visits are noted nor is there information to show who was
4 resident at the property at the time of service. Most important, as
5 pointed out by the Assessor, these written statements are not sworn
6 declarations, and there was no opportunity for the Assessor, or this
7 Board, to question these individuals regarding specific residency
8 issues. The Woodstone Credit Union data substantiates that Mr. Brabant
9 had an active account during 1999 and has had this account since 1988.
10 However, this is not probative of residency. Similarly, the King County
11 Regional Library card indicates Mr. Brabant has been a long- time card
12 holder, yet no information concerning his library activity during 1999
13 is furnished. As with the Credit Union account, this is not probative
14 of residency. None of the evidence carries the Appellant' s burden of
15 proof.
16
17 WAC 458- 16- 010( 1) sets forth the following items as considerations
18 for verifying residency: 1) ownership of another residence, 2) voter
19 registration, and 3) vehicle licensing. Item No. 1, ownership of
20 another residence, is included to identify possible residency alterna-
21 tives. Mr. Brabant owns two other properties, one a residence --his
22 Oak Harbor condominium. Regarding Item No. 2, voter registration, Mr.
23 Brabant provided a King County voter' s registration card. However, he
24 registered for this card on March 2, 2000, and it was issued on April 1,
25 2000, dates that fall after 1999. Accordingly, this evidence is not
26. probative of residency in 1999. Mr. Brabant furnished no evidence
27 regarding Item No. 3, vehicle licensing. By not submitting vehicle
INITIAL DECISION - Page 15 Docket No. 00- 068

1 licensing data, we can only infer that this evidence would not have
2 helped his case. Mr. Brabant did offer his driver' s license, which
3 reflects his Federal Way address. Yet, this license was issued on
4 April 6, 2001. As he did not provide his former license, which would
5 have included the relevant period of time, we can only infer that this
6 evidence also would not have helped his case.
7
8 Two other items were also included in this Board' s deliberations.
9 First, Ms. Busch states that during a June 26, 2000, visit to re -measure
10 Mr. Brabant' s Federal Way house, she saw no evidence of residency. In
11 rebuttal, Mr. Brabant provided photographs processed in August 2000 of
12 his home, showing some furniture items. These photographs depict only
13 minimal furniture. The weight accorded to both Ms. Busch' s testimony
14 and Mr. Brabant' s photographs is tempered by the timing in 2000.
15 Second, nearly all of the important documents submitted by Mr. Brabant
16 reflect his address as, PO Box 2064, Point Roberts, WA, a remote
17 location in Whatcom County where Mr. Brabant owns property and,
18 according to his testimony, spends only one night per year. Point
19 Roberts is a considerable distance from King County and accessible by
20 land only by driving through the Canadian Province of British Columbia.
21 These include IRS tax return documents, Social Security statements, and
22 Key Bank interest income statements. Also, Mr. Brabant' s 1999 interest
23 income statement from Woodstone Credit Union and his King County voter' s
24 registration card also reflect this Point Roberts' address.
25
26
27
INITIAL DECISION - Page 16 Docket No. 00- 068

1 Citing the portion of RCW 84. 36. 381( 1) that states confinement
2 to a hospital or nursing home is not grounds for exemption disquali-
3 fication, Mr. Brabant contends the time he spends in his Oak Harbor
4 condominium --a unit equipped for handicap living --should not count
5 against him. We disagree. While we understand the analogue Mr. Brabant
6 endeavors to draw, there is a significant difference between an indi-
7 vidually owned, handicap -equipped, condominium unit and a nursing home
8 or a hospital. RCW 84. 36. 381( 1) does not include handicap -equipped
9 residences when describing a consideration for time spent under care in
10 nursing homes and hospitals. Exemptions are not to be extended beyond
11 the scope clearly indicated by the Legislature. Mac Amusement Co. v.
12 Department of Revenue, 95 Wn. 2d 963, 633 P. 2d 68 ( 1981).
13
14 After weighing the evidence, we are unable to conclude that Mr.
15 Brabant, who bears the burden of proof in this matter, 4 resided at his
16 Federal Way property from January 1, 1999, and thereafter, as his
17 principal place of residence for more than six months during 1999.

1 2. 1 Within RCW 84. 36. 381 through 84. 36. 389, the Legislature
2 established the criteria whereby senior citizens qualify for property
3 tax exemptions.

5 2. 2 In relevant part, RCW 84. 36. 381 provides:
6 A person shall be exempt from any legal obligation to
pay all or a portion of the amount of excess and regular
7 real property taxes due and payable in the year following
the year in which a claim is filed, and thereafter, in
8 accordance with the following:
1) The property taxes must have been imposed upon a
9 residence which was occupied by the person claiming the
exemption as a principal place of residence as of the time
10 of filing: PROVIDED, That any person who sells, transfers,
or is displaced from his or her residence may transfer his
11 or her exemption status to a replacement residence, but no
claimant shall receive an exemption on more than one
12 residence in any year: PROVIDED FURTHER, That confinement
of the person to a hospital or nursing home shall not
13 disqualify the claim of exemption . . . .
14
15 2. 3 RCW 84. 36. 383 defines residence, in part as:
16 1) The term " residence" shall mean a single family
dwelling unit whether such unit be separate or part of a
17 multiunit dwelling, including the land on which such
dwelling stands not to exceed one acre.

25 1) . . . The residence must have been occupied by
the person claiming the exemption as the principal or main
26 residence of the claimant. It does not include a residence
used merely as a vacation home. For purposes of this exemp-
27 tion, principal or main residence means a residence the
claimant resides at or dwells in for more than six months

can be ownership of another residence, voter registration
2 and vehicle licensing.

a residence which was occupied by the person claiming the

9 4. 0 An exemption from taxation is to be construed narrowly.
10 Taxation is the rule and exemption is the exception." O' Leary v.
11 Department of Revenue, 105 Wn. 2d 679, 717 P. 2d 273 ( 1986). Exemptions
12 and deductions " are to be construed strictly in favor of the tax and, as
13 a corollary, they are not to be extended beyond the scope clearly indi-
14 cated by the legislature." Mac Amusement Co. v. Department of Revenue,
15 95 Wn. 2d 963, 633 P. 2d 68 ( 1981). Moreover, the taxpayer bears the
16 burden of establishing that it qualifies for the claimed exemption or
17 deduction. Group Health Coop. of Puget Sound, Inc. v. Department of
18 Revenue, 106 Wn. 2d 391, 401- 02, 722 P. 2d 787 ( 1986).
19
20 5. 1 A person claiming an exemption must meet the occupancy,
21 ownership, age, and income provisions set forth within RCW 84. 36. 381
22 through 84. 36. 389 and WAC 458- 16- 010 through 458- 16- 079.
